passage: Come, Deepak, sit by your Darshan Dada. You want to know how to help your friend? Let me tell you about Suresh. We were twenty, sharing a room in the college hostel, when his father's shop burned down. Suresh stopped going to class and lay facing the wall. I wanted to give him speeches. I even started to say, "When my mother died, I..." and stopped, because it wasn't about me. So I did small things. I brought his dinner from the mess. I sat on the floor with my books while he stared at the wall. Every evening I asked, "Walk to the tea stall?" Most days he said no. Some days, yes. After a month I told him, "I'm your friend, not a doctor. There's a doctor at the college clinic who talks with students. I'll come with you." He went. Fifty years later, Suresh still sends me mangoes every summer.

qa.q: What happened to Suresh's father's shop?
Why did Darshan stop in the middle of saying "When my mother died"?
qa.a: Dada caught himself, uneasy that comparing his own pain would make it about himself rather than Suresh.

qa.q: What choice did Dada make after a month?
qa.a: He admitted he was a friend, not a doctor, and offered to go with Suresh to the doctor at the college clinic.

qa.q: What might Dada's quiet company have meant to Suresh?
qa.a: Suresh likely felt he was not alone and not pressured, which made it easier to accept the tea-stall walks and later the clinic.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how he helped a struggling friend he shared a hostel room with by listening, keeping him company and bringing food, not lecturing or comparing pain, and nudging him to a doctor.

passage: Gurleen's own exams started on Monday, and the hostel wifi kept dropping. Still, every night at ten she called her friend Chaitanya in his city three hundred kilometres away, even if only for five minutes. Since he'd failed his second-year paper, he mostly spoke in short, flat sentences. On Wednesday he said, "Everyone else is moving on and I'm stuck." Gurleen felt a sharp flicker of resentment. She had her own paper in nine hours. Then she heard how tired he sounded and let it go. She didn't tell him about her cousin who had failed and bounced back, and she didn't list study tips. She only said, "That sounds really heavy. I'm here." On Thursday she found the number for his college counselling cell and sent it with one line: "I'm not a counsellor, but these people are. Want me to stay on the call while you book?" He did. The booking took four minutes.

qa.q: At what time did Gurleen call Chaitanya every night?
Why did Gurleen feel a flicker of resentment on Wednesday?
qa.a: Her own paper was in nine hours, and she was tired and stretched by giving time she needed.

qa.q: What choice did Gurleen make on Thursday, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: She sent the counselling cell's number and offered to stay on the call while Chaitanya booked, a small practical step toward professional help.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt hearing "That sounds really heavy. I'm here" instead of study tips?
qa.a: He may have felt heard rather than judged, which made him more willing to book the counsellor.

grounding: It shows a friend in exam week checking in daily, listening without comparing or lecturing, and giving a small practical nudge toward professional care.
